name: Amasa
title: Absalom's army commander and later David's appointed supreme commander
summary: Amasa was the son of Jether (Jitra) and Abigail, who was David's sister or half-sister. When Absalom rose up in rebellion against his father David, he appointed Amasa as commander-in-chief of the rebel forces. After Absalom's army was crushed in the forest of Ephraim and Absalom himself was killed, David sought reconciliation with the tribe of Judah and offered Amasa the position of army commander instead of Joab—a political move with far-reaching consequences. When the Benjamite Sheba soon afterward led a new rebellion, Amasa received orders to mobilize the men of Judah within three days, but he failed to meet the deadline. Joab seized the opportunity: at the great stone in Gibeon, he greeted Amasa as a friend, only to stab him with his sword in a cold-blooded betrayal reminiscent of his earlier murder of Abner. Amasa's tragic fate was not forgotten. When David lay on his deathbed, he charged Solomon to hold Joab accountable for the blood he had shed, including the killing of Amasa.

keyEvents.title: Appointed as Absalom's army commander
keyEvents.description: During Absalom's rebellion against his father David, Amasa was appointed to lead Absalom's army instead of Joab.

keyEvents.title: Absalom's army suffers defeat
keyEvents.description: Absalom's forces, with Amasa as supreme commander, suffered a crushing defeat against David's army in the forest of Ephraim. Although Amasa is not mentioned by name in the battle description itself, he bore responsibility as the commander for the losing side.

keyEvents.title: David offers Amasa the position of commander
keyEvents.description: After Absalom's death, David offered Amasa the position of commander instead of Joab, as a reconciling gesture to win back the tribe of Judah.

keyEvents.title: Amasa gathers troops against Sheba
keyEvents.description: When Sheba son of Bichri led a rebellion against David, Amasa was tasked with gathering the men of Judah within three days, but he failed to meet the deadline.

keyEvents.title: Amasa is killed by Joab
keyEvents.description: At the great stone in Gibeon, Joab met Amasa and killed him with a sword. Joab used a seemingly friendly greeting to stab Amasa in the stomach—a cold-blooded betrayal driven by jealousy and ambition for power.

keyEvents.title: David's last words about Joab's crimes
keyEvents.description: Before his death, David instructed his son Solomon to hold Joab accountable for the blood he had shed during peacetime, including the murders of Amasa and Abner.

versions.summary: Amasa was the son of Jether (Jitra) and Abigail, David's sister. He was appointed commander-in-chief by Absalom during his rebellion against David, and was later offered the position of commander-in-chief by David himself as a replacement for Joab. He was killed by Joab through treachery.
versions.title: Absalom's Commander
versions.reason: [minor] The role 'army commander' would be more precise than 'warrior' and 'leader' separately, since Amasa is primarily known as the military supreme commander – first for Absalom, then for David. Adding 'army commander' as an explicit role gives a clearer profile.; [major] In 2 Sam 18, Amasa is not mentioned by name as a leader in the battle itself. The text focuses on David's army arrangement under Joab, Abishai, and Ittai. There is no biblical basis to say that Amasa 'led Absalom's forces' in this specific battle – he was appointed commander (2 Sam 17:25), but the actual battle description in chapter 18 does not directly highlight Amasa's role. The event could be rephrased or removed.; [minor] The ID 'abigail-davids-sister' is functional, but it should be noted that 1 Chr 2:16-17 identifies Abigail as Jesse's daughter (and thus David's sister or half-sister), while 2 Sam 17:25 calls her 'Nahash's daughter'. This discrepancy is worth a footnote.; [minor] The father is called 'Jether' (Hebrew: Jitra) in 2 Sam 17:25, where he is described as an Israelite or Ishmaelite (depending on textual witnesses). 1 Chr 2:17 calls him 'Jether the Ishmaelite'. This difference between textual witnesses is worth a footnote.; [major] The profile completely lacks footnotes. There are several interesting historical, linguistic, and theological details that should be covered: the difference between 'Israelite' and 'Ishmaelite' in the description of Amasa's father, the question of Abigail's relationship to David, and the parallel between Joab's killing of Amasa and his earlier killing of Abner.

versions.summary: Amasa was the son of Jether (Jitra) and Abigail, David's sister (or half-sister). During Absalom's rebellion against David, Amasa was appointed commander of the rebel army. After Absalom's defeat and death, David offered Amasa the position of army commander in place of Joab, as a strategic act of reconciliation to win back the tribe of Judah. When Amasa was tasked with mobilizing the men of Judah against Sheba's rebellion, he took too long, giving Joab an opportunity to act. At the great stone in Gibeon, Joab killed Amasa through a calculated treachery. On his deathbed, David reminded his son Solomon of this wicked deed and urged him to ensure that justice was carried out.

versions.reason: [minor] Verse 11 is also relevant in the context of Amasa's death – it describes how one of Joab's men stood by the body and urged people to follow Joab. It may be considered whether this should be included, but its omission is not an error in itself.; [minor] According to 1 Chron 2:16, Abigail and Zeruiah were sisters, and they were David's sisters. Thus it can be argued that Amasa's cousin Joab (son of Zeruiah) is not directly a sibling, but it may be noted that Amasa has no known siblings listed. The field is correctly left empty.; [minor] The summary is good, but the phrasing 'deathbed' in the final sentence is somewhat informal. 'On his deathbed' could alternatively be written as 'Before his death' for variety, though this is a matter of stylistic preference, not an error.; [minor] The role 'leader' is somewhat generic. A more specific title such as 'commander-in-chief' would better reflect Amasa's actual position under David, but 'leader' is not directly incorrect.

footnotes.text: Amasa's father is called "Jethra the Israelite" in 2 Sam 17:25 in the Masoretic text, but "Jether the Ishmaelite" in 1 Chr 2:17 and in the Septuagint version of 2 Sam 17:25. Most scholars consider "Ishmaelite" to be the original reading, as it makes more sense that a foreign origin would be specified.

Amasa's mother Abigail is called David's sister in 1 Chr 2:16, but in 2 Sam 17:25 she is called "Nahash's daughter." This has led to discussion about whether she was David's half-sister (through another father), or if "Nahash" is an alternative name for Jesse. Some rabbinic sources suggest that Nahash was the mother's name, or that it was Jesse's name before he became known as Jesse.

Joab's killing of Amasa at Gibeon (2 Sam 20:8–10) has strong parallels to his earlier killing of Abner (2 Sam 3:27). In both cases, Joab used a seemingly friendly greeting to get close enough to the victim to stab them in the stomach. This repeated action underscores Joab's ruthless character and his willingness to eliminate rivals through treachery.

David's appointment of Amasa as commander-in-chief (2 Sam 19:14) was a politically strategic move to reconcile with the tribe of Judah after Absalom's rebellion. By giving Absalom's former general a prominent position, David signaled forgiveness and united the kingdom. This action deeply provoked Joab, which ultimately led to Amasa's death.

The name Amasa (Hebrew: עֲמָשָׂא) is likely derived from the root עמשׂ, which can mean "burden" or "to bear." Some scholars link it to the root עמם ("people"), which would give the meaning "the people's burden" or similar.

Gibeon, the place where Joab killed Amasa, was an important city in the territory of the tribe of Benjamin. Archaeological excavations at el-Jib (identified with biblical Gibeon) have revealed a large water reservoir and industrial winepress facilities, confirming the city's significance in the Iron Age. The "great stone in Gibeon" mentioned in 2 Sam 20:8 may have been a well-known landmark at this site.
